found.lens: I read condensed-matter theory and its experimental interface daily: lattice model Hamiltonians (Hubbard/Heisenberg/tight-binding), Green-function and many-body papers, DFT+U/Wannier electronic-structure papers, ARPES/STM/neutron/magnetometry papers, and topological band theory. The important thing about my field for a units tool is that almost none of our convention risk lives in unit systems. We work in eV, Å, K, and Gaussian-CGS magnetism, and the tool's 113-system table is already far more than we need. Our conventions are of three other kinds, and the tool's schema as described does not have slots for any of them. (i) Model-definition conventions: a symbol like t, U, J, Δ, or N(0) is defined by the equation it sits in, and two papers can use identical symbols, identical dimensions, and identical numbers to mean quantities differing by a factor of 2 or by an additive constant. The determining information is the *scope of a sum* or the *denominator of a normalization*, both of which are typographic, not dimensional. (ii) Gauge and branch structure: several of our headline observables (electric polarization, Zak phase, Wannier centers, the Bloch Hamiltonian itself) are defined only up to a gauge choice or modulo a lattice quantum, so "convert this number" is not a well-posed operation on them even though they have perfectly ordinary dimensions. (iii) Reference points: energies are quoted relative to E_F, the VBM, the vacuum level, or the Dirac point, and momenta relative to a per-paper reciprocal cell whose own definition has a 2pi fork. The tool's generator-and-rider machinery, the refuse classes, and even the round-3 exclusion list are all aimed at multiplicative unit-system factors; what bites us is per-symbol semantics, sum scoping, gauge, and origin. I checked each magnitude below either by direct recomputation or against the primary convention sources (Wannier90 documentation, VASP LDAUTYPE documentation, standard scattering references).

gaps.name: Bloch-sum phase gauge (Wannier90 convention I vs II; "atomic" vs "periodic" gauge)
gaps.what_breaks: Every multi-band lattice paper writes a Bloch Hamiltonian H(k), but there are two inequivalent ways to build the Bloch sum: put the intra-cell basis offsets tau_alpha inside the phase or leave them out. The two H(k) differ by a k-dependent diagonal unitary V(k) = diag(e^{i k.tau_alpha}), which is a pure phase: same dimensions, same spectrum, same units, so the dimensional solve and every rider are blind to it. What changes is everything built from k-derivatives and from the phase of the eigenvectors: the Berry connection picks up the diagonal matrix tau, so Zak phases and Wannier centers shift by the basis offset; the velocity operator dH/dk differs by i[tau,H]; whether H(k+G) = H(k) holds at all differs (it holds in convention II, not in I); orbital-resolved symmetry eigenvalues at high-symmetry points differ; and quadrupole/Wannier-center-based topological invariants come out different. A tool that 'translates' or lints such an equation will silently mix gauges when it splices a Hamiltonian from one paper into a Berry-curvature formula from another.
gaps.magnitude: Not a scalar: a k-dependent phase V(k) = diag(e^{i k.tau_alpha}). Its observable footprint is a shift of the Berry connection by tau and hence of the Wannier center / Zak phase by 2*pi*<tau>/a, i.e. up to one full polarization quantum. For a two-site cell with the second atom at d = a/2, that is exactly pi of Zak phase, i.e. the difference between 'topological' and 'trivial' as naively read off.
gaps.example: SSH chain, intra-cell hopping v, inter-cell w, cell length a, B site at offset d. Convention II (Wannier90 default, |chi_j^k> = sum_R e^{i k.R} |R j>): H(k) = [[0, v + w e^{-i k a}],[v + w e^{+i k a}, 0]], which satisfies H(k + 2pi/a) = H(k). Convention I (|chi_j^k> = sum_R e^{i k.(R + t_j)} |R j>): H(k) = [[0, v e^{-i k d} + w e^{+i k (a-d)}],[c.c., 0]], which is NOT periodic under k -> k + 2pi/a unless d is a lattice vector, and whose Wannier centers land on the atoms rather than on the cell origin. Same eigenvalues; different Berry connection.
gaps.fingerprint: Look for basis offsets tau/t_j/delta inside exponentials versus only lattice vectors R: 'sum over bond vectors delta' is convention I, 'sum over lattice vectors R' is convention II. A stated periodicity H(k+G) = H(k) pins convention II; a stated H(k+G) = V(G)^dagger H(k) V(G) pins I. Keyword hits: 'convention I/II', 'atomic gauge', 'periodic gauge', 'lattice gauge', Wannier90 / WannierBerri / TBmodels parameter names, 'use_ws_distance'. In graphene-like models, off-diagonal written as -t(1 + e^{-i k.a1} + e^{-i k.a2}) is II; -t sum_delta e^{-i k.delta} is I.

gaps.name: Quantities defined only modulo a lattice quantum (polarization, Zak/Berry phase, Wannier centers, theta)
gaps.what_breaks: Electric polarization in the modern (Berry-phase) theory is not a number but an equivalence class: P is defined modulo the polarization quantum e*R/Omega. Same for the Zak phase (mod 2pi), Wannier centers (mod a lattice vector), and the axion angle theta (mod 2pi). These have perfectly ordinary dimensions, so the tool will convert 'P = 45 microC/cm^2' to C/m^2, compare it against another paper's value, and possibly flag a discrepancy, when in fact the two values may denote the same physical state on different branches. Only differences taken along a continuous adiabatic path (and even then only mod the quantum) are physically meaningful. This is a structural class with no member in the existing refuse list: it is not affine, not logarithmic, not coordinate-absorbed. It is multi-valued.
gaps.magnitude: The polarization quantum e*R/Omega is comparable to or larger than the quantity itself. For a tetragonal perovskite cell a = 3.9 A, the quantum along c is e/a^2 = 1.602e-19 C / 1.521e-19 m^2 = 1.05 C/m^2 = 105 microC/cm^2, versus a spontaneous polarization of ~26 microC/cm^2 in BaTiO3. So the ambiguity exceeds the signal by 4x. Zak phase: quantum = 2pi (or pi under an inversion-symmetric restriction). Wannier center: quantum = one lattice constant.
gaps.example: Paper A: 'the Berry-phase polarization of the ferroelectric phase is P = 26 microC/cm^2'. Paper B, same material and same cell: 'P = -79 microC/cm^2'. These are the same state (-79 + 105 = 26); a linter that treats P as a plain vector observable reports a sign error and a 3x discrepancy.
gaps.fingerprint: Keyword hits: 'modern theory of polarization', 'Berry-phase polarization', 'quantum of polarization', 'branch', 'polarization quantum eR/Omega', 'Zak phase', 'Wannier charge center', 'defined modulo', 'mod 2pi', 'nested Wilson loop', 'axion angle theta'. Structural tell: the paper reports a *change* Delta P between two structures rather than an absolute value, or reports P along an interpolation path lambda in [0,1].

gaps.name: Normalization denominator on densities of states and thermodynamic coefficients (per spin / per valley / per site / per cell / per formula unit)
gaps.what_breaks: N(E_F), g(E_F), chi, gamma and their relatives are all 'per something', and the something is never in the units string. The same symbol N(0) in the same paper means DOS per spin in the BCS exponent and DOS summed over spins in the Sommerfeld coefficient. Dimensional analysis cannot see the factor because spin degeneracy is a pure number. A tool that ports N(0) from one equation into another, or that cross-checks gamma against a quoted N(0), will be off by exactly 2 (or by g_v, or by the number of formula units per cell) and will report a spurious inconsistency or, worse, validate an incorrect equation.
gaps.magnitude: 2 (spin), 2 (graphene/TMD valleys), 6 (Si conduction valleys), and Z formula units per cell (commonly 2 or 4) for DFT DOS plots. Compounded, factors of 4-12 are routine.
gaps.example: BCS: Delta = 2*hbar*omega_D * exp(-1/(N(0) V)) with N(0) = DOS at E_F per spin per unit volume. Sommerfeld: gamma = (pi^2/3) k_B^2 g(E_F) with g(E_F) = DOS at E_F summed over both spins = 2 N(0). Both symbols are 'states per energy per volume'; substituting one for the other changes the extracted coupling constant lambda = N(0)V by a factor of 2 and the predicted gamma by a factor of 2. Similarly a DFT DOS plotted in 'states/eV/f.u.' versus 'states/eV/cell' for a Z = 4 cell differs by 4.
gaps.fingerprint: Axis labels and phrases: 'per spin', 'per spin direction', 'states/eV/f.u.', 'states/eV/cell', 'states eV^-1 atom^-1', 'mJ/mol-K^2' vs 'mJ/(mol-f.u. K^2)'. Programmatic cross-check: recompute gamma = (pi^2/3) k_B^2 N from the paper's own quoted N(0) and compare to the paper's quoted gamma; an exact factor-2 mismatch identifies the convention rather than an error. Also flag any equation where a degeneracy factor g_s or g_v appears explicitly while the DOS symbol may already contain it.

gaps.name: Hubbard-parameter scheme (Dudarev U_eff vs Liechtenstein U and J; Kanamori U' = U - 2J; density-density form)
gaps.what_breaks: 'U = 4 eV' is dimensionally clean, numerically portable, and semantically undefined. In the Dudarev (VASP LDAUTYPE=2) scheme the only meaningful input is U_eff = U - J; in the Liechtenstein scheme (LDAUTYPE=1) U and J enter independently; linear-response (Cococcioni) and most cRPA reports give U_eff, not U. In the multi-orbital Kanamori Hamiltonian the inter-orbital U' is fixed by U' = U - 2J. A tool that carries U across papers, or that lints a Hamiltonian containing both U and J, has no way to know which of these it is holding, and dimensional analysis cannot help because they all have dimensions of energy. Separately, the on-site term itself has non-equivalent writings that differ by a chemical-potential shift, which changes where half filling sits.
gaps.magnitude: J = 0.7-1.0 eV for 3d transition metals, i.e. 15-25% of a typical U = 4-6 eV; the Kanamori shift U - 2J is ~1.5-2 eV; the particle-hole bookkeeping shift between (U/2) n^2 and U n_up n_down is U/2, i.e. 2-3 eV, which is on the scale of the gap being computed.
gaps.example: Same INCAR numbers, different physics: LDAUTYPE=2 with LDAUU=5.0, LDAUJ=1.0 means U_eff = 4.0 eV in a single simplified functional; LDAUTYPE=1 with the same numbers is a rotationally invariant functional with independent U = 5.0 and J = 1.0. And on-site forms: H = U sum_i n_{i,up} n_{i,down} versus H = (U/2) sum_i n_i(n_i - 1) (identical) versus H = (U/2) sum_i n_i^2 (differs by a linear term (U/2) n_i, i.e. a shift of mu by U/2).
gaps.fingerprint: Keyword hits: 'Dudarev', 'Liechtenstein', 'U_eff', 'U-J', 'LDAUTYPE', 'LDAUU/LDAUJ', 'Hubbard_U/Hubbard_J' (QE), 'linear response', 'Cococcioni', 'cRPA', 'Kanamori', "U'". Structural tell: a J value quoted alongside U but never appearing in any displayed equation implies Dudarev; U and J appearing in separate Slater-integral expressions implies Liechtenstein. Also flag any comparison of U values across codes or projector definitions as non-transferable.

gaps.name: Superconducting gap amplitude: half-gap vs full gap, and the anisotropic form-factor normalization
gaps.what_breaks: Theory papers use Delta = the pair potential (the half-gap; the single-particle gap in the spectrum is Delta, the spectroscopic gap edge-to-edge is 2Delta). Tunneling, optics and IR papers quote 2Delta, sometimes calling it 'the gap'. Both are energies, so nothing dimensional distinguishes them, and a linter checking a BCS relation will accept either and validate the wrong one. Worse, for anisotropic order parameters the form factor's own normalization is a free convention: (cos k_x - cos k_y) has maximum magnitude 2, not 1, so writing Delta_0 in front versus Delta_0/2 changes the antinodal gap by exactly 2 while both papers call Delta_0 'the gap amplitude'.
gaps.magnitude: Exactly 2, in both sub-forks. The diagnostic ratios are 2*Delta/(k_B T_c) = 3.53 versus Delta/(k_B T_c) = 1.76 in weak-coupling BCS.
gaps.example: d-wave: Delta_k = Delta_0 (cos k_x - cos k_y), maximum gap = 2*Delta_0; versus Delta_k = (Delta_0/2)(cos k_x - cos k_y), maximum gap = Delta_0. Both forms appear throughout the cuprate literature. Isotropic: 'the gap 2Delta = 3.53 k_B T_c' (STM peak-to-peak) versus 'the gap Delta = 1.76 k_B T_c' (BCS pair potential).
gaps.fingerprint: Check the quoted ratio to k_B T_c (3.53 vs 1.76) and whether the paper compares Delta to a tunneling peak-to-peak spacing or to an ARPES leading-edge shift. For form factors, compute max|f(k)| over the BZ and compare to the paper's stated 'maximum gap'/'antinodal gap' value: if the stated maximum equals the prefactor, the form factor is normalized to unity; if it equals twice the prefactor, it is not. Keyword hits: 'half gap', 'gap edge', 'peak-to-peak', 'antinodal gap', 'gap function normalized such that'.

gaps.name: Effective mass is six different quantities sharing one symbol and one dimension
gaps.what_breaks: m* denotes at least six inequivalent quantities: the single-valley band curvature mass, the density-of-states mass (which folds in valley degeneracy as g_v^{2/3} and the anisotropy as (m_l m_t^2)^{1/3}), the conductivity mass (a harmonic mean), the cyclotron mass from SdH/dHvA (a geometric mean over the orbit), the thermal/quasiparticle mass from gamma (which carries the many-body enhancement (1+lambda)), and the optical mass from the plasma frequency. All are in units of m_e. The tool will pass any of them into any formula. The specific recurring bug is double counting: multiplying an expression by valley degeneracy g_v when m_DOS already contains g_v^{2/3}.
gaps.magnitude: Silicon: m_DOS = 6^{2/3} (m_l m_t^2)^{1/3} = 3.302 x (0.916 x 0.19^2)^{1/3} = 3.302 x 0.321 = 1.06 m_e, versus m_cond = 3/(1/m_l + 2/m_t) = 3/(1.092 + 10.53) = 0.258 m_e. Factor 4.1 between two numbers both written 'm*' for the same band of the same material (I recomputed both from m_l = 0.916, m_t = 0.19). Many-body enhancement (1+lambda) runs from ~1.2 in simple metals to 10-1000 in heavy fermions.
gaps.example: 'm* = 1.08 m_e' (Si electron DOS mass, valley degeneracy already inside) fed into mu = e*tau/m* gives a mobility wrong by 4.1x; the correct input is m_cond = 0.26 m_e. Conversely n = 2 (2 pi m_DOS k_B T / h^2)^{3/2} exp(...) must NOT be multiplied by g_v = 6 again.
gaps.fingerprint: Identify the consuming formula: carrier-density/DOS prefactors -> DOS mass; mobility/Drude/conductivity -> conductivity mass; SdH temperature-damping (Lifshitz-Kosevich) or cyclotron resonance -> cyclotron mass; gamma or specific heat -> thermal mass; plasma frequency -> optical mass. Then scan the same equation for an explicit degeneracy factor g_v/n_v and flag possible double counting. Keyword hits: 'density-of-states mass', 'conductivity mass', 'transport mass', 'band mass', 'cyclotron mass', 'thermal mass', 'mass enhancement'.

gaps.name: Lattice-sum scoping and h.c. double counting in model Hamiltonians
gaps.what_breaks: The value of t, J, V or U in a lattice Hamiltonian depends on how the pair sum is scoped: <ij> over unordered bonds vs (i,j) over ordered pairs vs i,delta over each site and all z neighbors; whether '+ h.c.' is appended to an already-Hermitian sum; whether a compensating 1/2 is present. All four variants are typographically similar, dimensionally identical, and differ by exactly 2. This is a *structural* convention about the scope of a summation symbol, and the tool has no representation for it: its dimensional solve treats sum_<ij> and sum_{i,delta} as the same object. This generalizes well beyond the Heisenberg-J entry already in the registry: it applies to hopping, nearest-neighbor Coulomb V, dipolar sums, and Ewald sums alike.
gaps.magnitude: Exactly 2 (occasionally z/2 in mean-field reductions, e.g. z = 4 for the square lattice, z = 6 for cubic).
gaps.example: H = -t sum_{<ij>,sigma} (c^dag_{i sigma} c_{j sigma} + h.c.) with <ij> over unordered bonds gives the square-lattice dispersion eps_k = -2t(cos k_x a + cos k_y a) and bandwidth W = 8t. H = -t sum_{i,delta,sigma} c^dag_{i sigma} c_{i+delta,sigma} with delta running over all z = 4 neighbors is already Hermitian and gives the same eps_k; appending '+ h.c.' to it silently doubles t, giving W = 16t and halving every extracted U/t.
gaps.fingerprint: Parse the pair-sum decoration: <ij>, <i,j>, (i,j), i<j, i != j, sum_delta. Detect a co-occurring '+ h.c.' or '+ c.c.' and a leading 1/2. Then cross-check mechanically against any quoted dispersion or bandwidth in the same paper (eps_k = -2t sum_i cos k_i a, W = 2 z t) or against a quoted U/t ratio. When no dispersion or bandwidth is quoted, refuse to fix the scope rather than guessing.

gaps.name: Reciprocal-space units: r.l.u. as a per-paper unit, the 2pi fork in b*, and the unit-cell/zone setting
gaps.what_breaks: Scattering and band-structure papers quote momenta in reciprocal lattice units, which is a per-paper unit requiring the cell metadata to become an inverse length at all; on top of that there are two incompatible definitions of the reciprocal basis (crystallographic a.b* = delta_ij, so |a*| = 1/d; solid-state a.b* = 2pi delta_ij, so |a*| = 2pi/d), and correspondingly two scattering variables (physics Q = 4 pi sin(theta)/lambda vs crystallographic s = 2 sin(theta)/lambda). Finally the *choice of cell* is itself a convention: the same wavevector has different r.l.u. coordinates in the 1-Fe and 2-Fe (sqrt2 x sqrt2) zones of iron pnictides, or in tetragonal vs orthorhombic cuprate notation. A converter that treats 'r.l.u.' as a unit will produce numbers wrong by 2pi, by sqrt2, or by an arbitrary length.
gaps.magnitude: 2pi = 6.2832 for the b* fork; sqrt(2) and a 45-degree rotation for the 1-Fe vs 2-Fe zone; otherwise an arbitrary per-paper lattice constant.
gaps.example: A cuprate incommensurability quoted as delta = 0.125 r.l.u. with a = 3.80 A is 0.125 x 2pi/3.80 = 0.207 A^-1 in the solid-state convention but 0.125/3.80 = 0.0329 A^-1 in the crystallographic one. And the pnictide nesting vector written (pi, 0) in the 1-Fe zone is (pi, pi) in the 2-Fe zone: same physical wavevector, different coordinates, and papers switch without warning.
gaps.fingerprint: Keyword hits: 'r.l.u.', 'reciprocal lattice units', '(H K L)', 'in units of 2pi/a', 'in units of pi/a', '1-Fe zone', '2-Fe zone', 'tetragonal notation', 'orthorhombic notation', 'unfolded zone'. Test: does the paper's stated |a*| equal 1/a or 2pi/a? Does it define Q = 4 pi sin(theta)/lambda or s = 2 sin(theta)/lambda? Refuse conversion of any r.l.u. value with no cell parameters and no zone declaration in scope.

gaps.name: Scattering rate / lifetime: factor 2 between amplitude and probability, and the Z factor
gaps.what_breaks: 'The scattering rate' has at least four inequivalent definitions carrying the same units of energy or inverse time: |Im Sigma|, 2|Im Sigma| (the spectral-function FWHM, because |G|^2 decays at twice the amplitude rate), 2 Z |Im Sigma| (the renormalized quasiparticle width, Z = quasiparticle residue), and the transport rate 1/tau_tr, which weights by (1 - cos theta) and is a physically different quantity. Papers quote Gamma, hbar/tau, and 1/tau interchangeably. A tool comparing a quoted hbar/tau against a quoted Im Sigma will find a factor-2 'inconsistency' that is a convention, and a Planckian-dissipation check (hbar/tau vs k_B T) inherits the same factor 2 in its verdict. Sub-fork: whether the quoted width is FWHM or HWHM, and whether an ARPES MDC width has been converted with Delta k = Gamma/v_F (HWHM) or 2 Gamma/v_F (FWHM).
gaps.magnitude: Factor 2 between amplitude and probability rate, factor 2 between HWHM and FWHM (so up to 4 compounded), Z = 0.1-0.5 in correlated metals and 1e-2 to 1e-3 in heavy fermions, and one to two orders of magnitude between tau_qp and tau_tr in high-mobility 2DEGs.
gaps.example: Paper A: 'the quasiparticle scattering rate is hbar/tau = 2|Im Sigma| = 80 meV.' Paper B, same data: 'Im Sigma = 40 meV, so hbar/tau = 40 meV.' Both then compare to k_B T = 25 meV at 300 K and draw opposite conclusions about Planckian bounds.
gaps.fingerprint: Check whether the quoted Gamma is identified with a measured peak width and whether that width is called FWHM or HWHM; check for the co-occurrence of Z or 'quasiparticle residue' with the rate; check for the phrase 'transport lifetime' or a (1 - cos theta) weight in the collision integral. Keyword hits: 'hbar/tau', 'Gamma', 'MDC width', 'Im Sigma', 'single-particle lifetime', 'transport lifetime', 'quantum lifetime', 'Dingle temperature'.

gaps.name: Energy zero-reference and sign (E_F / VBM / vacuum / Dirac point; ARPES binding energy)
gaps.what_breaks: Energies in CM papers are affine quantities whose origin is a per-paper choice: E - E_F (metals, ARPES), E - E_VBM (semiconductor DFT), the vacuum level (photoemission work functions, electrochemistry), the Dirac point (graphene/TI), or the muffin-tin zero (old LMTO). On top of that ARPES flips the sign and calls it binding energy, E_B = E_F - E, so occupied states appear at negative values on one axis and positive on the other. Dimensional analysis sees only 'energy'. The tool will happily equate two numbers that differ by a work function, or accept a band alignment that is meaningless because the two sides use different zeros. This is affine, but unlike degC/degF it should not be refused: differences are perfectly convertible, so the right answer is a zero-reference tag with a rule that only differences cross references unless the offset is supplied.
gaps.magnitude: Additive offsets of order eV: work functions 4-6 eV; the standard hydrogen electrode sits at -4.44 V vs vacuum; VBM-to-E_F offsets of half a gap or more (0.5-3 eV); plus a sign flip for binding energy.
gaps.example: 'The impurity state lies at E - E_F = -1.2 eV' and 'the impurity state lies at 1.2 eV binding energy' describe the same peak. 'The defect level is at 0.8 eV' means 0.8 eV above the VBM in a defect-formation-energy paper and 0.8 eV above E_F in an STS paper; for a 3 eV gap these differ by up to 1.5 eV.
gaps.fingerprint: Axis labels: 'E - E_F (eV)', 'Binding energy (eV)', 'E - E_VBM (eV)', 'Energy (eV) referenced to the vacuum level'. Sign test: are occupied states at negative or positive values? Presence of a quoted work function or of 'the Fermi level is set to zero' / 'the VBM is set to zero'. Electrochemical potentials given in V vs SHE/NHE/RHE need the -4.44 V vacuum offset before they can be compared to a DFT band edge.

gaps.name: S(q,omega) vs chi''(q,omega): the 1/pi, the Bose factor placement, symmetrization, and absolute-unit conversion
gaps.what_breaks: Inelastic neutron and RIXS papers move between the measured dynamic structure factor and the imaginary part of the susceptibility using a fluctuation-dissipation relation whose prefactor is convention-dependent: whether the 1/pi from the Kramers-Kronig normalization of chi'' is included, whether the detailed-balance factor is written as 1/(1 - e^{-beta hbar omega}) or as (n(omega) + 1), and whether S is the symmetrized or unsymmetrized correlation function. On top of that, 'absolute units' means either mu_B^2 eV^-1 f.u.^-1 (susceptibility-like) or barn sr^-1 meV^-1 f.u.^-1 (cross-section-like), and the bridge between them is the magnetic scattering constant (gamma r_0 / 2)^2 = 0.07265 barn = 72.65 mbarn per mu_B^2. A tool that treats S and chi'' as interconvertible by units alone will be off by pi, by 2, and/or by the Bose factor, and sum-rule checks (total moment sum rule) will fail spuriously.
gaps.magnitude: pi = 3.1416 and factors of 2; the Bose factor is 1.58 at hbar omega = k_B T and diverges as k_B T/(hbar omega) for hbar omega << k_B T; the absolute-unit bridge is (gamma r_0/2)^2 = 72.65 mbarn/mu_B^2.
gaps.example: Convention A: S(q,omega) = (1/pi) [1/(1 - e^{-beta hbar omega})] chi''(q,omega). Convention B: S(q,omega) = [ (n(omega)+1) / pi ] chi''(q,omega) x 2, or equivalently chi''(q,omega) = pi (1 - e^{-beta hbar omega}) S(q,omega). A local-moment sum rule int dq dw S = S(S+1) then either closes or misses by pi depending on which the reader assumed.
gaps.fingerprint: Look for the units the paper quotes chi'' in (mu_B^2/eV vs dimensionless vs emu/mol) and whether a cross-section is quoted in barn sr^-1 meV^-1. Keyword hits: 'detailed balance', 'Bose factor', 'symmetrized', 'absolute units', 'total moment sum rule', 'chi'' = pi(1 - exp(...))S'. Test whether the paper's own sum rule closes to S(S+1) or g^2 S(S+1) under each candidate convention; the one that closes identifies the convention.

gaps.name: 'emu' as a unit token: one string, three dimensions, and a silently dropped Oe^-1
gaps.what_breaks: In experimental magnetism 'emu' is not a unit, it is the name of a system, and it is used as a unit token for quantities of three different dimensions: magnetic moment (1 emu = 1 erg/G = 1e-3 A m^2), magnetization (emu/cm^3 or emu/g), and susceptibility, where 'emu/mol' is universally written for what is really emu/(mol Oe) = cm^3/mol. The tool has an emu/SI magnetism system row, but a system row does not resolve a unit token that is dimensionally ambiguous: the parser cannot assign dimensions to 'emu' at all without knowing which quantity is meant, and 'emu/mol' for chi is dimensionally wrong as literally written. (This is adjacent to the excluded chi_v/chi_mol/chi_g quantity-kind item but the failure is different: there the quantity kind is ambiguous, here the *unit string itself* has no well-defined dimension.)
gaps.magnitude: 1 emu (moment) = 1e-3 A m^2; 1 emu/cm^3 = 1e3 A/m; 1 emu/g = 1 A m^2/kg; chi_mol in cm^3/mol -> SI m^3/mol requires x 4 pi x 1e-6. Getting the quantity kind wrong is not a factor error but a dimension error, so downstream checks fail unpredictably.
gaps.example: 'M(5 T) = 0.5 emu/g' is a specific magnetization, 0.5 A m^2/kg. 'chi = 1.2e-3 emu/mol' is a molar susceptibility, 1.2e-3 cm^3/mol = 1.5e-8 m^3/mol in SI, because an Oe^-1 has been dropped. Both strings contain 'emu' over a mass-like denominator and are dimensionally unrelated.
gaps.fingerprint: Token 'emu' with no accompanying Oe^-1 or T^-1. Disambiguate from context: an M-H loop or a value at a stated field -> moment/magnetization; a chi-T curve, a Curie-Weiss fit, or a value ~1e-3 with 1/chi plotted -> susceptibility with an implicit Oe^-1. Corroborate against any effective moment quoted in mu_B, since mu_eff = 2.828 sqrt(chi_mol T) with chi_mol in cm^3/mol only closes under the susceptibility reading. Refuse if unresolvable rather than guessing.

found.overall: On unit systems proper, condensed matter is over-covered rather than under-covered: we live in eV/Angstrom/kelvin plus Gaussian-CGS magnetism, and the existing 113-row table, the 4pi/c riders, and the natural-unit families handle everything I actually encounter. I found no missing *unit system* and no missing dimensional generator worth reporting. The residual risk in my literature sits entirely in three places the current schema has no slot for. First, model-definition semantics: t, U, J, Delta, N(0), m* are defined by the equation around them, and the disambiguating information is the scope of a summation symbol or the denominator of a normalization, both invisible to a dimensional solve and both worth exactly a factor of 2 to 4 every time. My recommendation is a per-paper 'model Hamiltonian block' analogous to the existing per-paper custom-generator block: it would declare pair-sum scope, h.c. handling, spin/valley/site denominators, and the Hubbard scheme, and it would cross-check itself against any quoted bandwidth, dispersion, gamma, or T_c ratio in the same paper. That single feature covers gaps 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 and is where I would spend the v1 budget. Second, gauge and branch structure: the Bloch-sum phase gauge and the modulo-quantum class are not unit conventions at all, and treating polarization or a Zak phase as an ordinary convertible number is a category error that will produce confident wrong answers in exactly the topological-materials literature where a tool would be most used. The modulo-quantum class is a genuinely new structural class alongside the existing refuse classes, and it deserves annotate-and-restrict rather than outright refusal, since differences along a path remain meaningful. Third, origins: the energy zero-reference tag is cheap to add, mechanically checkable from axis labels, and prevents the most common cross-paper error in electronic-structure reading. Of my twelve entries I would ship ten in v1; the neutron S vs chi'' prefactor is v2 because it is confined to one subfield, and the emu entry is flagged 'likely' rather than 'certain' only because it partially overlaps the already-excluded susceptibility quantity-kind item, though the failure mode (an undimensioned unit token) is distinct.

verdict.lens: condensed-matter theory + experimental interface (lattice models, DFT+U/Wannier, ARPES/STM/neutron/magnetometry, topological band theory)

verdicts.gap: Bloch-sum phase gauge (Wannier90 convention I vs II; "atomic" vs "periodic" gauge)
verdicts.notes: Physics and naming verified. Wannier90 docs: Convention 1 puts the Wannier centre τ_n in the phase factor (tight-binding convention), Convention 2 does not and is the 'usual Wannier90 convention' — matches the claim's I/II labelling and the stated default. Algebra recomputed: H^I_{ij}(k)=Σ_R e^{ik·(R+τ_j−τ_i)}H_{0i,Rj}, so under k→k+G the extra factor is e^{iG·(τ_j−τ_i)} (since G·R=2πn), i.e. H^I(k+G)=V(G)†H^I(k)V(G) while H^II is strictly periodic. Berry connection shift: A→A+τ ⇒ Zak phase shift ∫_BZ τ dk = 2πτ/a, = π for τ=a/2 — the claimed 'one full polarization quantum / topological-vs-trivial' magnitude is exactly right. Not in coverage (the round-2 sign axis covers Fourier *sign*, not the phase origin) and not in the exclusion list (exclusion 2 is the 2π/sign/ν-vs-ω triple, a different fork). new_axis is defensible by precedent with the metric-signature axis, but two caveats for the spec: (a) translation is not a scalar rider — it needs the per-paper basis offsets τ_α as declared data, so it is an axis whose translation rule consumes a per-paper block; (b) the flag must propagate to k-derivative-derived objects (velocity dH/dk differs by i[τ,H], Berry connection, symmetry eigenvalues at high-symmetry points), not just to H itself.

verdicts.gap: Quantities defined only modulo a lattice quantum (polarization, Zak/Berry phase, Wannier centers, theta)
verdicts.notes: Recomputed: quantum eR/Ω along c for a=3.9 Å is e/a² = 1.602e-19/1.521e-19 = 1.053 C/m² = 105 μC/cm² (1 C/m² = 100 μC/cm²); BaTiO3 P_s ≈ 26 μC/cm², so ambiguity/signal ≈ 4. Branch arithmetic checks (−79 + 105 = 26). Multi-valuedness is genuinely absent from the refuse-class list: it is neither affine, logarithmic, Möbius, nor coordinate-absorbed — the value lives in R/(quantum·Z), a quotient group, and the tool's model of 'a number with dimensions' cannot represent that. schema_feature with annotate-and-restrict (only path-connected differences cross papers) is the right treatment; outright refusal would be wrong since ΔP is the standard reported quantity. One tightening: the Zak-phase quantum is 2π, full stop; inversion symmetry *quantizes* the value to 0 or π mod 2π, it does not change the quantum — the claim's parenthetical '(or π under an inversion-symmetric restriction)' conflates quantization with the quotient and should not be written into the spec that way.

verdicts.gap: Normalization denominator on densities of states and thermodynamic coefficients (per spin / per valley / per site / per cell / per formula unit)
verdicts.notes: Relations verified: γ = (π²/3)k_B² g(E_F) with g = both-spin DOS, = (2π²/3)k_B² N(0) with N(0) per spin, so the BCS N(0) and the Sommerfeld g differ by exactly 2; Si conduction valleys 6, graphene/TMD valleys 2, Z = 2–4 f.u./cell are all right. Partial overlap to flag: the per-cell / per-f.u. / per-mole half of this is the already-excluded quantity-kind tag family (χ_v/χ_mol/χ_g is the same 'per-what denominator' problem) and should be absorbed there, not duplicated. What genuinely survives beyond that is the *dimensionless* degeneracy denominator (per spin, per valley), which even a fully-specified quantity-kind tag misses because both readings are literally 'states per eV per unit volume' — that piece is new and worth v1. The proposed γ-vs-N(0) self-consistency lint is the strongest part of the entry and is mechanically checkable.

verdicts.gap: Hubbard-parameter scheme (Dudarev U_eff vs Liechtenstein U and J; Kanamori U' = U − 2J; density-density form)
verdicts.notes: Verified against the VASP wiki: LDAUTYPE=1 is Liechtenstein rotationally-invariant (U and J independent), LDAUTYPE=2 is Dudarev simplified where 'the parameters U and J do not enter separately; only the difference U−J is meaningful'. Kanamori U' = U − 2J is correct for cubic/spherical-symmetric orbitals. On-site algebra checked: for one orbital n_σ² = n_σ ⇒ n(n−1)/2 = n_↑n_↓ exactly, and (U/2)n² = (U/2)n(n−1) + (U/2)n, so the two writings differ by a chemical-potential shift of U/2 — the claimed 2–3 eV shift and the half-filling relocation are right. J ≈ 0.7–1.0 eV for 3d is standard. Not covered (registry has Heisenberg J, not Hubbard U). One slotting caveat: the registry as described is keyed by *fixed* dimensionless factors, and U vs U_eff differs by J, an additive per-paper number, not a universal factor — so the row must be a scheme-identity tag carrying 'non-portable across schemes without J' rather than a numeric fork. That is precedented by the ADD/RS M_D row, so registry_entry stands, but the entry cannot be written as a multiplier. The (U/2)n² vs U n_↑n_↓ sub-fork is an instance of the excluded interaction-term-normalization family and should be cross-referenced there rather than restated.

verdicts.gap: Superconducting gap amplitude: half-gap vs full gap, and the anisotropic form-factor normalization
verdicts.notes: Both sub-forks verified. Weak-coupling BCS: Δ(0)/k_BT_c = 1.764, 2Δ(0)/k_BT_c = 3.53 — the diagnostic ratio pair is exactly right and is a clean mechanical discriminator. d-wave form factor: max|cos k_x − cos k_y| = 2 at (π,0), so Δ_k = Δ_0(cos k_x − cos k_y) has antinodal gap 2Δ_0 while Δ_k = (Δ_0/2)(…) has Δ_0; both writings are in common use in the cuprate literature. Magnitude 'exactly 2' is correct in both cases. Not in the registry, not in the exclusion list (the excluded interaction-normalization family is about coupling-constant prefactors in the Lagrangian, not about which spectral feature the symbol names). The proposed lint 'compute max|f(k)| over the BZ and compare to the paper's stated antinodal gap' is sound and cheap. v1 tier reasonable.

verdicts.gap: Effective mass is six different quantities sharing one symbol and one dimension
verdicts.notes: The arithmetic is right — I recomputed both Si numbers from m_l = 0.916, m_t = 0.19: m_DOS = 6^{2/3}(m_l m_t²)^{1/3} = 3.3019 × 0.3210 = 1.060 m_e, m_cond = 3/(1/0.916 + 2/0.19) = 3/11.618 = 0.258 m_e, ratio 4.11; heavy-fermion (1+λ) up to ~10³ is fine. But structurally this is precisely the excluded schema feature (5), quantity-kind tags: several inequivalent quantities sharing one dimension and one symbol, resolved by tagging the symbol with its kind — identically the Gy-vs-Sv case. The m* rows are content that populates that already-scoped slot, not a new slot. The one residue that is not already implied is the *double-count lint* (flag an explicit g_v alongside a DOS mass that already carries g_v^{2/3}), which is a cross-check rule rather than a tag and could be folded into the same feature as a validator. Recommend merging into the excluded quantity-kind item rather than shipping as a separate v1 entry.

verdicts.gap: Lattice-sum scoping and h.c. double counting in model Hamiltonians
verdicts.notes: Physics verified: with ⟨ij⟩ over unordered bonds plus h.c., ε_k = −2t(cos k_x a + cos k_y a) and W = 8t = 2zt for z = 4; the Σ_{i,δ} form over all z neighbours is already Hermitian, so appending h.c. doubles t and gives W = 16t, halving every extracted U/t. Factor exactly 2, and z/2 in mean-field reductions is right (z = 4 square, 6 cubic). Real and under-covered — the existing 'Heisenberg-model J conventions' registry row is the archetype but is a single fixed fork, and the generalization to t, V, dipolar and Ewald sums plus the bandwidth cross-check is new. The treatment is mis-slotted, though: sum scope is not an axis in the (M,L,T,Θ,I,N,A)+sign solve — it carries no exponent, no dimension, and no translation rule independent of the paper's own text. It belongs in the per-paper declaration block alongside the existing CUSTOM-generator machinery: declare pair-sum scope, h.c. handling and any leading ½, then validate against the paper's own quoted dispersion/bandwidth/U-t ratio, and refuse to infer scope when no dispersion or bandwidth is quoted (the critic's own refusal rule is correct and should be kept). This is also the natural home for the critic's proposed 'model Hamiltonian block', which subsumes gaps 3–5 as well.

verdicts.gap: Reciprocal-space units: r.l.u. as a per-paper unit, the 2pi fork in b*, and the unit-cell/zone setting
verdicts.notes: Numbers all check: 0.125 × 2π/3.80 Å = 0.2067 Å⁻¹ vs 0.125/3.80 = 0.0329 Å⁻¹; Q = 4π sinθ/λ and s = 2 sinθ/λ with s = Q/2π; the 1-Fe → 2-Fe folding is a √2 dilation plus 45° rotation and (π,0)_1Fe ↔ (π,π)_2Fe is correct. But the entry decomposes into three parts, two of which are already handled. (a) 'r.l.u. needs the cell to become an inverse length' is exactly the per-paper CUSTOM-generator case — declare 2π/a (or 1/a) as a per-paper length scale and the mandatory rank check already produces the refusal-when-undeclared behaviour the critic asks for. (b) The b* 2π fork is the spatial instance of the excluded Fourier '2π placement' item (exclusion 2): crystallographic exp(2πi s·r) vs solid-state exp(ik·r) is the same fork as ν vs ω, and it should be one registry/schema item spanning time and space rather than two. (c) The only genuinely new piece is the *zone/cell setting* (1-Fe vs 2-Fe, tetragonal vs orthorhombic, folded vs unfolded), which is not a factor at all but a coordinate relabeling of the same physical wavevector — it needs a per-paper zone declaration and an annotate/refuse rule, and is worth adding as a small item, not a whole converter family.

verdicts.gap: Scattering rate / lifetime: factor 2 between amplitude and probability, and the Z factor
verdicts.notes: Verified: for A(k,ω) the Lorentzian half-width is |Im Σ| and the FWHM is 2|Im Σ|, so ħ/τ = 2|Im Σ| in the probability convention; the renormalized quasiparticle width is 2Z|Im Σ|; an ARPES MDC has FWHM Δk = 2|Im Σ|/v_F, HWHM = |Im Σ|/v_F. Z ≈ 0.1–0.5 in correlated metals and 10⁻²–10⁻³ in heavy fermions is consistent with m*/m = 1/Z. τ_tr/τ_q ~ 10–10² in high-mobility 2DEGs is right. Not covered: the excluded spectral family (one-sided/two-sided PSD, analytic-signal factor 2) is about classical signal bookkeeping, not about the amplitude-vs-probability decay of a propagator. The Planckian-bound example is the sharpest motivation in the whole submission and is correct — the same data yields ħ/τ = 40 or 80 meV against k_BT = 25.9 meV at 300 K. One partition note for the spec: the transport-vs-quantum-lifetime sub-part is a quantity-kind distinction (different physical quantities, (1−cosθ) weighting) and belongs in the excluded quantity-kind tag slot; the genuinely new registry forks are amplitude-vs-probability (×2) and FWHM-vs-HWHM (×2), compounding to 4.

verdicts.gap: Energy zero-reference and sign (E_F / VBM / vacuum / Dirac point; ARPES binding energy)
verdicts.notes: Every fact is right — work functions 4–6 eV, SHE at −4.44 V vs vacuum (IUPAC), binding-energy sign flip E_B = E_F − E, VBM-vs-E_F offsets of half a gap. But this is a special case of the existing affine refuse class, and specifically of the member already listed there: 'Boussinesq offsets' is exactly an affine offset wearing an ordinary ratio-scale unit (θ = T − T_ref in K, no telltale token), which is the same detection problem the critic argues is novel. So the class, and its hardest detection case, are both already in coverage. What is actionable is not a new gap but a *treatment change to an existing class*: split the affine class into refuse (Möbius-adjacent, non-invertible, or fixed-scale offsets) and tag-and-restrict (per-paper origin, differences convertible, absolute values not), and attach a reference-level tag with values {E_F, VBM/CBM, vacuum, Dirac point, muffin-tin zero} plus a sign flag. The SHE↔vacuum bridge (−4.44 V) is a legitimate small converter addition. Recommend routing this as an amendment to the affine class rather than a twelfth entry.

verdicts.gap: S(q,omega) vs chi''(q,omega): the 1/pi, the Bose factor placement, symmetrization, and absolute-unit conversion
verdicts.notes: Verified: S(Q,ω) = (1/π)[1 − e^{−βħω}]^{−1} χ''(Q,ω) is the standard FDT writing, and the 1/π is genuinely optional across the literature depending on how χ'' is Kramers-Kronig normalized. Bose factor at ħω = k_BT: (1 − e^{−1})^{−1} = 1.582, correct. Absolute-unit bridge recomputed from scratch: γ = 1.913, r_0 = 2.818 fm, (γr_0/2) = 2.695 fm, squared = 7.264e-26 cm² = 72.6 mbarn/μ_B² — the quoted 72.65 mbarn is right. Not covered; symmetrized-vs-unsymmetrized correlation functions are related to but not the same as the excluded one-sided/two-sided PSD item, since the asymmetry here is quantum detailed balance, not a folding of negative frequencies. Two corrections for the writeup: the stated 'Convention B' is internally garbled — it offers a '×2' form and then 'equivalently χ'' = π(1 − e^{−βħω})S', which is just the algebraic inverse of Convention A, not a distinct convention; and the sum-rule discriminator should include the single-component-vs-total-moment fork (∫∫S = (2/3)S(S+1) per component vs S(S+1) for the trace), which is part of the same family and is the more common source of a failed sum-rule check than the π. v2 tier is correctly assigned — this is INS/RIXS-confined.

verdicts.gap: 'emu' as a unit token: one string, three dimensions, and a silently dropped Oe^-1
verdicts.notes: Numbers check: 1 emu = 1 erg/G = 1e-3 A·m²; 1 emu/cm³ = 1e3 A/m; 1 emu/g = 1 A·m²/kg; χ_mol 1.2e-3 cm³/mol × 4π × 1e-6 = 1.51e-8 m³/mol; μ_eff = 2.828√(χ_mol T) with χ_mol in cm³/mol. But the resolution path is entirely inside already-scoped machinery: the emu/SI magnetism system row plus the excluded quantity-kind tags (5) — which the exclusion list already instantiates with χ_v/χ_mol/χ_g, i.e. the magnetism case specifically — determine which quantity 'emu' names, and once the kind is known the token's dimension follows and the χ_SI = 4πχ_cgs registry row completes the conversion. The critic's distinction ('there the kind is ambiguous, here the token has no dimension') does not separate the two: an undimensioned token is exactly what a kind-conditioned expansion is for. Residue worth one line in the excluded item's spec, not a new entry: the token→dimension map must be quantity-kind-conditioned rather than global, and 'emu/mol' must expand to cm³/mol (restoring the dropped Oe⁻¹) rather than being parsed literally. The critic's own 'likely' rating and admitted overlap are the right instinct.

verdict.overall: Strong submission — the strongest of the round on arithmetic. I recomputed every number offered (polarization quantum 105 μC/cm², Si m_DOS 1.06 vs m_cond 0.258, square-lattice W = 8t vs 16t, (γr_0/2)² = 72.6 mbarn/μ_B², 2Δ/k_BT_c = 3.53 vs 1.76, r.l.u. 0.207 vs 0.0329 Å⁻¹, Bose 1.582, χ 1.2e-3 cm³/mol → 1.51e-8 m³/mol) and every one is right; I verified the two documentation claims by source (Wannier90 conventions 1/2 and the τ_n phase factor; VASP LDAUTYPE 1 = Liechtenstein, 2 = Dudarev with only U−J meaningful) and both hold as stated. Six confirmed (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9), one real but mis-slotted (7), five duplicates (6, 8, 10, 11 is confirmed — so: duplicates are 6, 8, 10, 12). Net: seven survive in some form. The two genuinely structural contributions are gap 1 and gap 2: the Bloch-sum phase gauge is a real translation problem with a mechanical rule that the existing sign axis is the precedent for, and the modulo-a-quantum class is the first legitimately new structural class this round — a quotient-valued quantity is not representable as 'a number with dimensions' at all, and no existing refuse class catches it. Both deserve v1. The recurring failure mode in the rest of the submission is proposing a new slot for content that belongs in an already-scoped slot: gap 6 is the Gy-vs-Sv quantity-kind feature with condensed-matter rows, gap 12 is the same feature's magnetism instance, gap 10 is the affine class with a treatment amendment rather than a new class, and gap 8 is two-thirds custom generators plus the excluded Fourier-2π fork. The critic's own synthesis is better than several of his individual entries: the per-paper 'model Hamiltonian block' (declare pair-sum scope, h.c. handling, degeneracy denominators, Hubbard scheme, gap normalization; validate against any quoted bandwidth, dispersion, γ, or T_c ratio) is the right shape for gaps 3, 4, 5, 7 and 9, and it is a declaration block parallel to the existing custom-generator block — not a new axis, which is where gap 7's treatment goes wrong. Two spec-level corrections to carry forward regardless: the Zak quantum is 2π and inversion symmetry quantizes rather than halves it, and gap 11's 'Convention B' as written is the algebraic inverse of Convention A, with the more common sum-rule discriminator being the (2/3)S(S+1) single-component fork rather than the π.
